opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to think about it is that the ratio of tokens to parameters ends up mattering a lot more than people had assumed, and it matters in a direction that's a little counterintuitive.

The standard intuition has been: more pre-training data is always better. You train longer, you get a better base model, and everything downstream should improve. And on the pre-training loss itself, that's basically true. But when we looked at what happens after pre-training, whether you quantize the model to lower precision or fine-tune it for some downstream task, we started seeing that models trained on a very large number of tokens relative to their size become more fragile.

On the precision side, what we found is that post-training quantization degrades the model more the longer you've pre-trained it. So if you take a fixed model size and keep increasing the token count, at some point the extra data actually makes the quantized model worse. You've packed so much information into the weights that small perturbations, which is essentially what quantization is, become more damaging. So there's a sort of tension: the more you squeeze out of each parameter, the less slack you have.

And we see something analogous with fine-tuning, which we've been calling catastrophic overtraining. If you over-train a smaller model, it can get harder to adapt. When you fine-tune it, you can see worse performance downstream, and also more forgetting of the capabilities it had from pre-training. The way we've been thinking about it is in terms of sensitivity: as you train longer, the parameters become progressively more sensitive to modifications, and both quantization and fine-tuning are modifications. So a heavily over-trained model can actually end up in a worse place after you do anything to it.

So the relationship isn't "more tokens is better, period." It's that for a given model size, there's a point beyond which extra tokens buy you a better base model on paper but a model that's less robust to the things you actually do to it in practice. Larger models can absorb more tokens before hitting that regime, so the sweet spot shifts with scale, but the effect is there.

The practical takeaway is that when you plan a training run, you shouldn't optimize only for pre-training loss. You should think about the whole pipeline: are you going to serve this in low precision, are you going to fine-tune it heavily? If so, the compute-optimal or even inference-optimal choice of tokens per parameter may look different from what you'd pick if you only looked at the base model.

r001.rationale: It describes quantization degradation increasing as token count rises for a fixed model size, directly tying the precision result to tokens relative to parameters.

r002.rationale: It mentions downstream tasks generally but does not state that the fine-tuning trend depends on the dataset of interest.

r003.rationale: It says larger models can absorb more tokens before reaching the regime where extra training makes them less robust, in the context of fine-tuning effects.

r004.rationale: It emphasizes the tokens-to-parameters ratio and says the sweet spot shifts with scale, but does not state that the fine-tuning relationship need not follow that simple ratio.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this came out of work we did on scaling laws for precision, and the key variable turns out to be the ratio between the two, not either one alone. What we care about is how many tokens you've trained on relative to the number of parameters. When that ratio is small, you're in the regime most people are used to: the model is undertrained relative to its size, and quantizing it after the fact, say to int4 or int3, costs you very little. The weights have a lot of slack in them.

What surprised us is what happens as you keep pushing that ratio up. If you take a fixed model size and just keep feeding it more pre-training data, post-training quantization gets progressively worse. Past some point, the degradation from quantizing actually outweighs the benefit of the extra tokens. So you can end up in a situation where training on more data makes your quantized model worse than if you'd stopped earlier. That's a counterintuitive result, because the whole industry trend is toward overtraining small models on enormous token counts, which is exactly the regime where this bites hardest.

The intuition is that as you overtrain, the model is using more of its representational capacity. The weights become more sensitive, more finely tuned, and that fine structure is precisely what low precision destroys. So the relationship is roughly that quantization sensitivity grows with tokens per parameter.

On the fine-tuning side, the story is related but a bit different. When you fine-tune, you're making small, targeted changes to the weights, and those changes are often smaller than the quantization granularity. So if you're going to quantize, the ordering and the precision at which you do the fine-tuning matter a lot. Fine-tuning in low precision, or quantization-aware fine-tuning, behaves much more gracefully than fine-tuning in full precision and then quantizing, and again that gap widens for heavily overtrained models.

The practical takeaway is that if your deployment target is low precision, you should factor that into the compute-optimal allocation up front. The right model size and token budget shift once you account for the precision you'll actually serve at, and in many cases that pushes you toward a somewhat larger model trained on fewer tokens than the standard scaling laws would suggest.

r002.rationale: It discusses fine-tuning behavior but does not say the trend depends on the dataset of interest.

r003.rationale: It does not compare larger and smaller models or state that larger models tolerate more pre-training tokens before an inverse fine-tuning effect.

r004.rationale: Calling the fine-tuning story “a bit different” does not clearly state that its relationship between token count and model size need not follow their simple ratio.

astra-6.text: I’d characterize it as an interaction: model size alone doesn’t tell you how sensitive a model will be to reduced precision or how it will respond to fine-tuning. You also have to ask how many tokens it was pre-trained on relative to its size. A smaller model trained for a long time can behave differently from a larger model trained on the same number of tokens. So the useful lens is how much training the model has received relative to its capacity, rather than parameter count in isolation.

r002.rationale: It does not say that the fine-tuning trend depends on the dataset of interest.

sol-6.1.text: The important quantity is really the number of pre-training tokens relative to the model size. You can have two models with the same number of parameters, but if one has been trained on many more tokens, they can behave quite differently when you reduce precision or fine-tune them. What we find is that these more heavily trained models tend to be more sensitive to those perturbations. So model size alone doesn’t tell you how much precision you need or how robust the model will be to fine-tuning; you also have to account for how much pre-training it’s had.
